lessons.title: Deferred cleanup order
lessons.summary: If n becomes 3 instead of 2, what is printed?
explanation: defer schedules a call for when the surrounding function returns, including during panic unwinding. Arguments to the deferred call are evaluated when defer executes, not later.

Multiple deferred calls run in reverse scheduling order. This makes defer useful for cleanup, but a defer inside a long loop still waits for the whole function to return. Close errors may need explicit handling; defer is not proof that cleanup succeeded.

Complete local Go example; the app itself does not execute it:
```go
package main
import ("fmt")
func main() {
 n := 1
 defer fmt.Println("first", n)
 n = 2
 defer fmt.Println("second", n)
 fmt.Println("body", n)
}
```

Expected output or behavior: body 2
second 2
first 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Panic recovery boundaries
lessons.summary: If panic("broken") is replaced by fmt.Println("normal"), what prints?
explanation: panic stops normal execution and unwinds the current goroutine, running deferred calls. Prefer returned errors for expected failures. recover can stop a panic only when called directly in a deferred function in that panicking goroutine.

After recovery, the panicking function does not resume at the panic statement. It returns to its caller once deferred work finishes. With no active panic, recover returns nil. This small boundary prints a recovery message and lets main continue; it is not a policy of hiding arbitrary faults.

Expected output or behavior: recovered
after. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Type sets and constraints
lessons.summary: If Add is called with two float64 values, what happens?
explanation: An interface used as a constraint may specify a type set. The union ~int | ~int64 permits types whose underlying type is int or int64. ~ includes defined types with that underlying type; plain int alone would not include a distinct defined type. An interface with these type-set terms is used as a constraint, not as an ordinary variable type.

The compiler permits + because every allowed type supports it. type Count int defines a distinct type with underlying int, so Count satisfies this constraint. These small values avoid overflow; the constraint does not provide checked arithmetic.

lessons.title: Modules and local dependencies
lessons.summary: If Double is implemented as n * 3 instead, what prints after rebuilding?
explanation: go.mod records the module path and Go language requirement. Imports use module paths, while package names are identifiers used in source. A module can contain several packages.

A require records a dependency version; replace can redirect that module to a local directory. Save the files below and run go run . with GOTOOLCHAIN=local and GOPROXY=off to prevent toolchain or dependency downloads. A replacement needs the local module’s own go.mod; it is not copied into the main module automatically.
```text
// go.mod
module example.test/app
go 1.27.0
require example.test/math v0.0.0
replace example.test/math => ./localmath
// localmath/go.mod
module example.test/math
go 1.27.0
// localmath/math.go (Go source)
package math
func Double(n int) int { return n * 2 }
```
Expected output or behavior: 12. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.summary: If Twice returns n + 2 instead, what happens when the test runs?
explanation: A file ending _test.go can contain tests named TestXxx(t *testing.T). The testing package supplies t; t.Fatalf records failure, formats a message and stops that test. go test runs tests; go run does not.
Expected output or behavior: 6. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Add cases for zero and a negative value while keeping inputs small enough to avoid overflow. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

analogy.limit: A small example isolates one rule; production programs require further testing.

steps: Read one visible idea at a time.
Predict the changed case before choosing.
Explain the consequence, then optionally try the local transfer.

quiz.question: If Twice returns n + 2 instead, what happens when the test runs?
choices: The test is ignored unless main calls it.
The test passes because the function name is unchanged.
quiz.explanation: The recorded expectation remains six while the changed implementation computes five, so the assertion exposes the regression.

hints: Return to the preceding idea and compare what changed.
lessons.externalNotes: Go Core v1 uses the verified Go1.27.3 toolchain and standard library. The app supplies concept reading and an understanding check, not a Go browser runner. Local compiler results are recorded separately and do not certify learner mastery.
